Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details:
- What the test does
  - It integrates the trivial ODE y' = 1 from t = 0 to 30 with a DormandPrince853Integrator and two event handlers:
    - ResettingEvent at t = 10.99
    - ResettingEvent at t = 11.01
  - The test’s ResettingEvent.g(t, y) checks that the times at which g is evaluated never go backward relative to the last event that has already been triggered. If g is called with a time t that is less than lastTriggerTime, it asserts.

- Symptoms from the failing assertion
  - The assertion inside ResettingEvent.g complains about “going backward in time”, i.e., after an event has already been triggered at some time τ, another g evaluation happens with a time t < τ. This matches the reported bug: “Incomplete reinitialization with some events handling … the second one becomes unable to find its way.”

- How EventState drives event detection
  - EventState.evaluateStep(...) scans the current step [t0, t1] by subdividing it and calling the wrapped handler’s g at times determined from:
    - The internal EventState start-of-step time t0 and value g0 (lines 207–215).
    - The provided step interpolator for the current integrator step.
  - Crucially, evaluateStep always starts scanning at ta = t0 (line 207), and builds sub-step times tb from t0 (lines 212–214, 267–268). So if t0 is stale, g will be evaluated at obsolete times.

- Expected reinitialization after an event
  - When a step is accepted, EventState.stepAccepted(t, y) is supposed to reset internal state:
    - t0 is set to the accepted time t, and g0 is recomputed (lines 298–299).
    - For the handler that actually triggered at time t, previousEventTime and g0Positive are adjusted and eventOccurred is called (lines 301–306).
    - For other handlers, g0Positive is simply recomputed and nextAction is CONTINUE (lines 307–309).
  - EventState.reset(t, y) only clears the “pending event” flags (lines 329–341); it does not adjust t0/g0.
  - EventState.reinitializeBegin(interpolator) resets t0 and g0 from the interpolator’s previous time (lines 154–179). This must be called when starting a new substep after accepting an event and possibly resetting the state.

- What goes wrong with two events in the same integrator step
  - Consider a single integrator step that spans both event times, e.g., a step covering [9, 12].
  - Both event states detect potential events during evaluateStep:
    - One at 10.99, the other at 11.01.
  - The integrator picks the earliest pending event and truncates the step at 10.99. At this point, correct behavior requires:
    - Calling stepAccepted on all EventState instances, so that their t0 is updated to 10.99.
    - If any handler requested a RESET_STATE, restarting the event detection for the remainder of the step with all EventState instances fully reinitialized (via reinitializeBegin on all of them) so that subsequent scans start at t = 10.99.
  - The issue report’s “incomplete reinitialization” indicates that after the first event is accepted and the state is reset, not all EventState instances are fully reinitialized. Practically, either:
    - stepAccepted is only called for the handler that triggered, or
    - reinitializeBegin is not called for all handlers when continuing the remainder of the step.
  - Because EventState.evaluateStep starts from its internal t0 field, any handler that was not reinitialized still has t0 at the original step start (e.g., 9.0). As a result, its evaluateStep will call handler.g at times ta/tb < 10.99, i.e., earlier than the already-triggered event time.
  - This directly triggers the test’s assertion in ResettingEvent.g: it sees t < lastTriggerTime (which has already been set to the first event’s trigger time), and fails with “going backward in time!”

- Why the code allows this to happen
  - EventState.stepAccepted is the place that updates t0 and g0 (lines 298–309), but that only helps if it is called for all handlers when a step is truncated at an event time.
  - EventState.reset only clears flags; it leaves t0/g0 untouched (lines 329–341).
  - EventState.reinitializeBegin recomputes t0/g0 from the step interpolator’s “previous time” (lines 154–179), but must be invoked after a reset before scanning the remainder of the step.
  - If the integrator fails to invoke stepAccepted and reinitializeBegin for all EventState instances after handling the first event, some EventState objects retain a stale t0 from before the event and will evaluate g at obsolete times when searching for the next event in the same step.

- Conclusion
  - The failure is caused by incomplete reinitialization of the event handling state across multiple EventState objects when multiple events occur within the same integration step and the first event triggers a reset. The non-triggering EventState still uses stale t0/g0, so evaluateStep evaluates g at times prior to the already-accepted event time, causing “backward in time” calls and derailing the detection of the second event.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
